text: Chapter twelve, the chat system. Let's follow one message on its way to the person who needs to read it.

How does the server hand a new message to the recipient? The simplest way is polling. The client asks every so often, and most of the time the answer is empty. Long polling is better: the request stays open until a message arrives or it times out. But held-open requests cost resources, and after each reply the client has to ask again.

WebSocket takes a different approach. The client and server open one persistent connection, and either side can send data at any time. When a new message arrives, the server simply pushes it. No asking. So this design uses WebSocket for both sending and receiving.

The system has two kinds of services. Stateless services handle login, signup, and profiles. Through service discovery, they also recommend a chat server to the client. The chat server is stateful, because it holds the user's WebSocket connection. Beside it sit a presence service, a notification service, and a key-value store that keeps the chat history.

Now a one-to-one message. User A sends it to chat server one. The server assigns a unique message ID and writes the message to the key-value store. If B is online, it forwards the message to chat server two, which holds B's connection, and pushes it to B. If B is offline, a push notification is sent instead.

A message ID must be unique, and it must also be sortable. A global sixty-four-bit sequence, like Snowflake, could work. But clock drift makes it only roughly ordered. A more practical choice is a per-conversation sequence number. It only has to increase within one conversation. There's no need for one global order across all conversations.

A user may have several devices. Each device remembers its own cur max message ID, the newest message it already has. When a device comes online, it asks the store for messages with a larger ID, and fills in what it missed while offline. A dropped connection doesn't lose any messages.

A group chat has at most one hundred members. When someone sends a message, the system copies it, or an index entry for it, into every member's inbox. That makes syncing simple for each person. The cost is write amplification: the bigger the group, the more copies each message needs.

Online status relies on heartbeats. The client sends one to the presence service every five seconds. If none arrives for thirty seconds, the user is marked offline. A brief network hiccup won't take them offline right away. Note that this is only approximate. A weak network or a sleeping device can also trigger the timeout.

Status changes must reach friends. The approach is publish and subscribe. A has one channel with each friend: A with B, A with C, A with D. When A goes online or offline, the update is published to all three channels. Each friend subscribes to their own channel and receives it. This works when the number of friends is small.

Remember three things. WebSocket is the real-time channel, the message store is the history, and the cursor catches up after a disconnect. Order only has to hold within a conversation, and online status is an approximation.
